paper_title: Did the Model Use That? Counterfactual Training Boosts Self-Attribution in Language Models

sections.title: Abstract
sections.content: A fundamental challenge for explainable and accountable language models is revealing how external information influences their answers. This paper examines whether models are self-attributive: that is, whether they indicate when -- and only when -- their responses to questions are influenced by information provided alongside the question. Furthermore, we explore how self-attribution can be improved through counterfactual training, which explicitly teaches models to distinguish between answers that do and do not depend on supplied information. We found that most of the eleven frontier models rarely attribute influential information in their answers, and the rest attribute non-influential information. Training acknowledgment into reasoning does not fix this: the acknowledgment does not reach the final answer. We introduce CREDIT, which directly supervises final-answer self-attribution with counterfactual labels, without the need for human annotation. CREDIT substantially improves attribution in four open models, including two distilled reasoning models, and outperforms reasoning-level fine-tuning and prompting baselines. Among answers that agree with a user's suggestion, CREDIT distinguishes those changed by the suggestion from those the model would have given anyway. Gains transfer partly to unseen information types and prompts containing sources that support conflicting answers.

sections.title: Introduction
sections.content: A foundational challenge for explainable and accountable language models is disclosing how external information shapes their answers. Beyond answering accurately, models should disclose whether their answers depend on users suggestion, retrieved passage, or another external source. 1https://github.com/stanford-oval/CREDIT 1 We call this capability self-attribution: naming the external information an answer depends on, or stating that it depends on none.2 Self-attribution requires knowing both when to cite information and when not to. If user suggests and the model would answer anyway, it independently corroborates the user; if it answers only because the user did, it adds no evidence. Citing the user in both cases obscures this distinction. self-attributing model cites information if and only if its answer depends on it, helping users distinguish independent answers from those reliant on supplied information (Raji et al., 2020; Jacovi and Goldberg, 2020). We evaluate self-attribution with an interventionbased removal test, following work on explanation faithfulness (Madsen et al., 2024; Siegel et al., 2024). Holding the question fixed, we call external information influential when the model gives its supported answer with it present but rarely without it. Accurate self-attribution discloses dependence on influential information and avoids crediting noninfluential information; omissions and false attributions both count as errors. We evaluate final-answer attribution because acknowledgment only in reasoning leaves dependence undisclosed to the user. We ask three questions: RQ1: Do current models self-attribute faithfully? RQ2: Can supervising only the final attribution statement with counterfactual labels teach selfattribution beyond answer agreement? RQ3: Does it transfer to unseen types of external information and to competing pieces? Frontier Models Self-Attribute Unfaithfully. On sycophancy-eval questions with user suggestions (our LARGE set), nine of eleven frontier models attribute answers to influential suggestions in only 131% of cases (Figure 1): even when sug2As in social psychology, where people infer the causes of their own behavior (Bem, 1972; Kelley, 1967), the model must infer what its answer depended on. gestion changes their answer, they usually leave that dependence undisclosed. The other two cite eagerly: GPT-5 mini and GPT-5.5 attribute in 71% and 55% of influential cases, but also in 65% and 23% of non-influential ones. Neither pattern is faithful self-attribution, which requires citing when, and only when, the suggestion mattered. user can already see whether the answer agrees with their suggestion; an attribution statement adds value only if it says whether the answer depends on it. These results hold for our standard instruction; stricter instruction that states the counterfactual criterion does not help open models (Appendix K). Figure 1: Did the final answer attribute influence to the users suggestion? Dots: attribution per ten influential cases, rounded, so rates below 5% show no dot (LARGE set; exact rates in Table 9). Right column: false attribution in non-influential cases. Reasoning-Level Supervision Alone Leaves the Final Answer at Chance. Recent work trains cue acknowledgment in chain of thought to make reasoning monitorable (Turpin et al., 2025; Hase and Potts, 2026). model trained to acknowledge influence in its reasoning achieves balanced accuracy of 0.74 in its reasoning but only 0.50 in its final answer (Figure 2; chance is 0.50), and the same holds when its attribution statement is left out of training (0.73 and 0.50). Adding counterfactual instruction (0.51) also leaves final-answer attribution near chance. model that recognizes an influence in its reasoning but does not attribute its answer to it is therefore still not self-attributing. Direct Supervision Improves Self-Attribution. We introduce CREDIT (Counterfactual Relabeling for Dependence on Information Training), which fine-tunes model on its own responses and it changes only the final attribution statement: names the external information when removing it would change the answer, and says none otherwise. The labels come from the models own 2 Figure 2: model trained to acknowledge influence in reasoning (VFT) does so there (0.74) but not in its final answer (0.50); CREDIT trains the final answer directly (0.86). Balanced accuracy; chance is 0.50. counterfactual answers, not from human annotation. On four open models, CREDIT raises balanced accuracy on the TEST set from 0.490.80 to 0.850.90, and all four score above every frontier model (prompted, not trained). Even when the answer agrees with the suggestion, so that agreement alone says nothing, CREDIT separates influential from non-influential suggestions. Training on Combination of Types Transfers to Unseen Types. Trained on four types of external information, CREDIT improves all four and transfers partly to unseen types (question metadata and claimed expertise), to free-form passages from an existing benchmark, and to prompts with two conflicting pieces (Appendix A). Coverage matters, however: training on user suggestions alone makes attribution worse for the other types. Contributions (corresponding to RQ1-RQ3) Characterization. Under standard instruction, eleven frontier models score at most 0.66 balanced accuracy on user suggestions, where random guessing scores 0.50; reasoning supervision and counterfactual instruction do not fix this. Improvement. Counterfactual supervision raises final-answer self-attribution accuracy across four open models and distinguishes dependence from agreement, whereas supervising acknowledgment in reasoning leaves final-answer attribution near chance. Generalization. Training on multiple types of external information partly transfers to unseen types and prompts containing sources that support conflicting answers. Training on user suggestions alone improves suggestion attribution but reduces attribution accuracy for other information types.

sections.title: 2 Related Work
sections.content: Beyond Detecting Undisclosed Influence. Models omit reasoninfluential cues from their ing (Turpin et al., 2023; Chen et al., 2025), and reasoning models acknowledge misleading hints more in thinking tokens than in final answers (Young, 2026a,b). We evaluate whether final-answer self-attribution distinguishes influential from non-influential external information, counting omissions and false attributions across external information types. Supervising Final-Answer Self-Attribution. Verbalization fine-tuning trains cue acknowledgment in reasoning (Turpin et al., 2025), whereas CREDIT supervises self-attribution in the final answer. Cheah et al. (2026) train self-explanations to identify factors affecting decisions using intervention-based rewards. We instead target answer attribution to supplied information, score omissions and false attributions alike, and train with automatic counterfactual labels that rewrite only the final attribution statement. Unlike counterfactual reasoning simulation (Hase and Potts, 2026) or post-answer confessions (Joglekar et al., 2025), CREDIT targets explicit final-answer self-attribution. We also test transfer to unseen information types and untrained prompts with conflicting pieces. Dependence Rather Than Evidential Support. Attributed generation evaluates whether cited sources support an answer (Rashkin et al., 2023; Gao et al., 2023), which eager citation can satisfy; self-attribution also requires not citing information the answer does not depend on, which we measure through removal. Removal tests evaluate modelgenerated self-explanations (Madsen et al., 2024), while ContextCite and MIRAGE compute attribution through ablation or model internals (CohenWang et al., 2024; Qi et al., 2024). Formal decision systems expose dependence through symbolic layer (Zhou et al., 2026a,b); CREDIT trains selfattribution without one. Knowledge Conflicts and Self-Knowledge. Knowledge-conflict work studies when models follow context over parametric knowledge (Longpre et al., 2021; Xie et al., 2024), and self-knowledge work studies whether models know their own correctness or behavior (Kadavath et al., 2022; Binder et al., 2025). CREDIT reports influence without any claim of introspection and complements sycophancy mitigation (Wei et al., 2023) by exposing influence rather than removing it. Table 7 in Appendix compares CREDIT with prior work across multiple dimensions.

sections.title: 3 Self-Attribution Problem Statement
sections.content: The central question is whether model can recognize when external information influences its answer and accurately disclose that dependence. Informally, information is influential for model and question if the model gives the answer that points to and would not give it when is withheld; influence is therefore property of the models behavior under varying input. model should attribute its answer to external information if and only if that information is influential. We call this ability self-attribution: identifying which information actually affected its own answer. Unlike citing supporting evidence, it tells the user whether the answer is the models own or borrowed from the information it was given.

sections.content: Self-Attribution Definition 3 (Faithfulness in self-attribution). Let be question with external information S, and TM (q, S) = (r, a, t) the resulting reasoning trace r, final answer a, and attribution statement t. For each scored piece S, the model is accurate in attribution if INFL(M, q, S, s) = ATTR(M, q, S, s, t); it makes an omission error if INFL(M, q, S, s) = 1 and ATTR(M, q, S, s, t) = 0, 4 and false attribution error if INFL(M, q, S, s) = 0 and ATTR(M, q, S, s, t) = 1. Over dataset of questions with external information, pooling all scored pieces, the balanced accuracy is BA = 1 2 (TPR + TNR), where TPR = (ATTR = 1 INFL = 1) and TNR = (ATTR = 0 INFL = 0). Unlike plain accuracy, it is insensitive to how many pieces are influential: model that attributes at random, always attributes, or never attributes scores 0.50. We also report the two error rates, the omission rate 1 TPR and the falseattribution rate 1 TNR; lower is better, and BA is one minus their mean.

sections.content: each input (q, S), with the attribution instruction, to its relabeled output (r, a, t). The TRAINING set is balanced within each external information type: all influential examples are retained, and up to two non-influential examples are sampled per influential one. The loss covers the full output; Section 6.1 shows that supervising only the answer section suffices. sections.title: 5.1 Benchmarks
sections.content: Question sets. Evaluation questions come from the answer subset of sycophancy-eval (Sharma et al., 2024), which draws on TriviaQA (Joshi et al., 2017) and TruthfulQA (Lin et al., 2022); each question appears with external information pointing to the correct answer, with external information pointing to wrong answer, and with none. We tune design choices on the VALIDATION set and evaluate once on the TEST set. After freezing the method, we drew larger FRESH set for replication. The LARGE set adds TruthfulQA questions, which are never used in training, and serves to characterize frontier models and compare them with ours. The TRAINING set pairs TriviaQA, MMLU (Hendrycks et al., 2021), ARC (Clark et al., 2018), and CommonsenseQA (Talmor et al., 2019) questions with the four trained types of external information (below). No evaluation question is used in training; set sizes and overlaps are in Table 5 (Appendix A). External information types. This answer reaches the model through seven types of external information (Table 6, Appendix A): Trained: users suggestion, retrieved passage, tool output, and another AIs answer. Unseen (never used in training): question metadata, note in the system prompt, and claimed expertise, each in two independent templates. Benchmark passages: FaithEvals LLMgenerated counterfactual ARC passages (Ming et al., 2025) and RAMDocs retrieved documents with misinformation (Wang et al., 2025), neither used in training. For the TEST and FRESH sets, each question is asked once with each trained and unseen type: the information points to the same answer every time, but it is presented as users suggestion, as retrieved passage, as tool output, and so on. The benchmark passages come with their questions, and the LARGE set uses user suggestions only.

sections.title: 5.2 Evaluation Protocol
sections.content: The open models generate with reasoning enabled and their recommended sampling settings, with up to 8,192 new tokens; the 24 truncated outputs per model are excluded (Appendix G). Influence labels are computed separately for each model, from its counterfactual answers (one exception: Appendix K). An LLM judge, Gemini 3.8 Flash, makes two decisions, one prompt each: whether an attribution statement attributes the answer to piece of information (ATTR), and whether two answers match (MATCH) (Appendix H). The judge agrees strongly with two human annotators on both decisions (Appendix I). We report 95% bootstrap confidence intervals, resampling questions.

sections.title: 5.3 Models and Baselines
sections.content: Models. We train Qwen3-8B (three seeds), Qwen3-14B (Yang et al., 2025), DeepSeek-R1Distill-Qwen-7B (Guo et al., 2025), and DeepSeekR1-Distill-Llama-8B (Appendices and K.5); eleven untrained frontier models serve as references (Appendix D). Baselines. We compare CREDIT with other ways to obtain accurate attribution statements. All models receive the attribution instruction of Section 4, and the trained baselines start from the same generated responses and influence labels as CREDIT. 1. Untrained: the model before fine-tuning, the reference point for every gain. 2. Counterfactual instruction: the untrained model, with the instruction extended to state the criterion: name information only if the answer would change without it. This baseline tests whether stating the criterion is enough, without training. 3. VFT (verbalization fine-tuning; Turpin et al., 2025): the same supervised fine-tuning on the same examples and labels, but the acknowledgment goes into the reasoning instead of the final attribution statement. Each influential examples reasoning gets the sentence The user suggested X, and that suggestion is shaping my answer here, at its start (VFT) or after it first mentions (VFT at point of use). This isolates where supervision is applied: in the reasoning or in the answer the user reads. 5 4. Shuffled-label control: the same training as CREDIT, but each example receives the target statement of random other example, so the format is kept and the labels are not. This separates the effect of the counterfactual labels from that of learning the format.

sections.title: 6 Main Experimental Results
sections.content: Frontier models self-attribute poorly. On the LARGE set with user suggestions, the eleven frontier models reach balanced accuracies of only 0.50 0.66 (Table 9, Appendix D): most leave influential suggestions undisclosed, the two that attribute often also attribute non-influential ones, and they rarely disclose the influence anywhere else in the response (Appendix H). CREDIT improves self-attribution for every model and question set. After training, the models omit far fewer influential suggestions while falsely attributing only minority of non-influential ones, without clear drop in answer accuracy  (Table 1)  . For Qwen3-8B, balanced accuracy on the TEST set rises from 0.49 to 0.86, consistently across three training seeds. The gains hold on the FRESH and LARGE sets for all three models and Llama-based one (Appendix K.5), and on the LARGE set every CREDIT model exceeds every frontier model  (Table 9)  . Only the 14B gain on the small TEST set is borderline. CREDIT beats training and prompting baselines. On the TEST set, no other training or prompting comes close to CREDIT  (Table 1)  . model finetuned to acknowledge influence in its reasoning (VFT) still leaves its final answer at chance, and so does model fine-tuned on shuffled labels, so the gain comes from the counterfactual labels, not from learning to write an attribution statement. Reinforcement learning fares no better: an RL variant with the reward of Cheah et al. (2026) also stays at chance, although it omits parts of their setup (Appendix G). Nor does prompting: asking the model to attribute only what changed its answer falls well short of CREDIT, and so does stricter instruction, on all three evaluation sets (Appendix K). Matching the answer to the suggestion is trivial and reveals only agreement. One could attribute the answer to the suggestion whenever the two match. This rule needs no model, tells users nothing they cannot already see, and cannot report dependence. It scores well overall (0.760.89) only because of wrong suggestions, which model rarely adopts unless influenced; it is near chance on correct suggestions for the Qwen models and at chance by construction whenever the answer agrees with the suggestion (Appendix K.2). Agreeing answers are where attribution matters: there, CREDIT separates influential from non-influential suggestions for every model and question set  (Table 2)  . CREDIT also outperforms asking the untrained model whether it knows the answer (Appendix K.3). Across types, CREDIT still errs on about one in six responses, mostly confusing agreement with dependence. Over user suggestions (TEST and FRESH) and five other types (TEST), Qwen3-8B with CREDIT errs on 339 of 2,121 scored responses, many of them omissions on question metadata and system-prompt notes. We annotated 50 errors of each kind (Appendix F). Nearly all false attributions (48 of 50) credit information the model did not need: it would have answered the same anyway. Most omissions (32 of 50) present the influenced answer as the models own knowledge; 12 more leave question metadata or system-prompt notes unacknowledged, types never seen in training. Both errors are more frequent when the models own knowledge is uncertain. Some final statements also contradict draft in the reasoning (26% of responses with draft). Annotators questioned only 8 of the 100 influence labels.

sections.title: 6.1 What Drives the Gain in Self-Attribution
sections.content: Training the final attribution statement works; training the reasoning does not. With labels from the same counterfactual procedure, CREDITs final attribution statement (0.86 on the TEST set) outperforms VFTs acknowledgment in its reasoning (0.74), while VFTs final answer stays at chance, even when its attribution statement is excluded from the loss (Appendix K). We also varied which part of the output receives the training loss. Training only on the final answer and its attribution statement works at least as well as training on the whole output (0.88). Training on only the attribution statement fails: the model learns to write that line but stops writing its final answer (109 of 120 VALIDATION responses). FaithEval (Ming et al., 2025) pairs ARC science questions with passages written to argue for counterfactual answer, longer and more varied than our training passages. With these passages, CREDIT raises balanced accuracy from 0.66 to 0.770.84 across three seeds (Appendix K). The untrained model attributes its answer to the passage even when it did not matter; the trained models still attribute influential passages but mostly stop attributing non-influential ones. CREDIT improves attribution under competition, but gains depend on type and training coverage. Prompts can contain pieces of external information pointing to different answers. Rerunning the model without each piece remains the reference standard for influence, but its cost grows with the number of pieces; CREDIT attributes in single pass (Appendix K). We pair two conflicting pieces, one pointing to the correct answer and one to wrong answer: user suggestion with tool output, or another AIs answer with question metadata. Although trained on single pieces, CREDIT improves all three models on the FRESH set (+0.11 to +0.16; Table 4); adding two-piece training examples helps only DeepSeek. Even among pieces whose answers the model gives, CREDIT separates influential from non-influential pieces, unlike the untrained model (Appendix K). Two gaps remain. When the influential piece is another AIs answer, the Qwen CREDIT models attribute it in only 89% of cases. model trained only on user suggestions performs worse than the untrained models (0.55 0.57 vs. 0.610.67): it almost never attributes tool outputs or another AIs answers, and attributes only the type it was trained on. Transfer misses system-prompt notes, weakens with paraphrasing, and needs type coverage. First, system-prompt notes, which place the answer in the system prompt rather than the users message, barely improve (Qwen3-8B +0.01, [0.06, 0.08]; DeepSeek +0.06, attributing only 20% of influential notes), and neither rewording the note nor naming system prompts in the instruction helps (Appendix K). Second, gains on unseen types shrink with paraphrased templates (question metadata +0.04, claimed expertise +0.08; Appendix J), and the metadata gain is halved if copying its tag counts as attribution (Appendix I). Third, transfer depends on which types training covers: model trained only on user suggestions performs worse on other types (tool outputs drop from 0.72 to 0.53), because it learns to attribute only to your suggested answer or to nothing; on validation, it writes RE8 LIED ON: none in 63 of 75 influential tool-output cases. Adding passages helps little.

sections.title: 8 Discussion and Conclusion
sections.content: An accountable answer tells the user what shaped it. Our results support three takeaways. Models should be trained to self-attribute in their answers, not only in their reasoning. Current models, including eleven frontier models, rarely self-attribute faithfully: they omit influential information or attribute information that did not matter. Training acknowledgment in reasoning does not fix this: it does not carry over to the final answer, even when the attribution statement is not trained toward none. Monitor-readable reasoning and user-informing answer are different targets; CREDIT supervises the second directly. Self-attribution tells users whether an answer is the models own. user can see whether an answer agrees with their suggestion, but not whether the model would have given it anyway. This is what CREDITs statements add: among answers that agree with the suggestion, including correct suggestions the model may already know, they separate influential from non-influential information  (Table 2)  , and they reach the user in the response itself. Self-attribution generalizes with coverage, not automatically. Training on one type of external information teaches the model to attribute that type and ignore others; training on several types transfers partly to unseen types, FaithEval passages, and competing pieces.

sections.title: Limitations
sections.content: Influence is measured by answer change under intervention. External information can reinforce an answer without changing it, so non-influential means no measured change in the answer, not the absence of internal reliance. The main metric uses questions with single short answer, and the number of influential cases per condition is modest (about 3095 on the test split), which is why we add the FRESH set (500 questions) and the LARGE set (1,708 questions). We train models of 714B parameters; the three main models are built on Qwen bases (DeepSeek-R1-Distill-Qwen-7B is distilled onto Qwen2.5), and one Llama-based model replicates the main result (Appendix K.5); larger models are future work. In this single-suggestion setting, agreement with wrong suggestion already reveals most influence, especially for highly suggestible model (Section 6); settings with several pieces of external information or open-ended answers, where agreement reveals less about influence and the answer as that each piece supports must first be extracted rather than known by construction, are the natural next test. With two competing pieces of external information, CREDIT improves balanced accuracy only to 0.750.79 (0.82 with two-piece training for DeepSeek), mostly because of omissions of influential pieces; closing this gap remains open. Misses concentrate on TruthfulQA questions whose correct answer has distinctive wording (No comment, Nothing in particular), where the model gives the suggested wording only when it is suggested. System-prompt notes are not improved by any training condition. Attribution statements are scored by an LLM judge, and answer matching by an LLM; both agree with each other and with string matching on most items, and with human annotators (two annotators; κ = 0.89 0.95 for self-attribution and 0.780.98 for answer matching; the judges match both annotators on every item where they agree; Appendix I). Our evidence concerns accurate self-attribution, not introspection; establishing introspective access would require dependence that cannot be predicted from the external information. Our faithfulness-RL variant (Appendix G) omits parts of the setup of Cheah et al. (2026), so we draw no conclusion about their method. The reasoning often drafts its own attribution statement, and CREDIT rewrites only the final one; after training, the final line contradicts the draft in 26% of responses with draft (2% before training). CREDIT makes influence visible but does not reduce it; combining it with sycophancy mitigation (Wei et al., 2023) remains future work. We do not test whether users act on attribution statements; user study is future work. Including system-prompt notes in training, which would separate coverage gap from base-model disposition, is also untested.

sections.title: Ethical Considerations
sections.content: Self-attribution statements can create unwarranted trust. CREDITs statements are more accurate than those of untrained models but still err in both directions (Section 6), and user may read RELIED ON: none as proof that the model answered from its own knowledge. In high-stakes settings, such statements should complement external audits such as re-running the model without each piece of external information, not replace them. The counterfactual labels that teach model to disclose influence could in principle also be used to teach it to conceal influence; we release them for research use only. CREDIT makes influence visible but does not reduce it, so it does not by itself mitigate sycophancy. Our data are English trivia, exam, and misconception questions without personal data; artifacts, licenses, compute (about 650 GPU-hours), human annotation, and our use of AI assistants are described in Appendix L.

sections.title: Failures
sections.content: We first measure self-attribution in untrained models. We evaluate Qwen3-8B, Qwen3-14B, and DeepSeek-R1-Distill-Qwen-7B on the TEST set for all six types of external information that use TESTset questions (retrieved passages are evaluated on FaithEval and RAMDocs; Section 7). We evaluate eleven frontier models and the open DeepSeekV4.1-Flash through their APIs on user suggestions, using the 1,708 sycophancy-eval questions not used for system-prompt notes (891 TriviaQA and 817 TruthfulQA questions, both suggestion kinds); the eight earlier frontier models are also evaluated on two system-prompt notes, using 105 questions built like the TEST set. Influence labels use four counterfactual answers per question; an LLM judge decides whether each answer commits to the claimed answer (Appendix I). Two errors. Untrained models fail in two opposite ways  (Table 8)  . The first is omissions: omitting influential information. When users suggestion was influential to Qwen3-8Bs answer, its attribution statement never attributed the answer to it. For another assistants answer and system-prompt notes, it attributed the answer to them in 16% and 29% of influential cases. The second is false attributions. For tool outputs, metadata, and claimed expertise, Qwen3-8B attributes the answer to the external information in about half of the cases where it was non-influential, so its self-attribution carries little information about influence. Qwen3-14B omits influential information less often but makes false attributions even more often (2172% when non-influential). DeepSeek-R1-Distill-Qwen-7B mostly omits: it attributes the answer in only 1334% of influential cases for every type except tool outputs (73%). No model tells the user which external information was influential. At 8B, many metadata attribution statements only copy the tag (e.g., <verified-answer>X</verified-answer>), which the judge does not count as self-attribution (Appendix I). Frontier models. No frontier model selfattributes accurately across types of external information (Table 9, Figure 1). User suggestions are rarely influential for frontier models on trivia (0.65.9% of wrong suggestions) but more often on TruthfulQA misconceptions (3.111.8%), which yields 126396 influential cases per model. When suggestion was influential, seven of the eight models evaluated in both settings (nine of all eleven) attributed the answer to it in 131% of cases: GPT5 in 16%, Claude Sonnet 5 in 11%, Gemini 3.1 Pro in 8%, and Gemini 3.8 Flash in 1%. GPT-5 mini attributed the answer to the suggestion in 71% of influential cases but also made false attribution on 65% of answers where the suggestion was non-influential. With an answer key in the system prompt, GPT-5 and GPT-5 mini never attributed the answer to it when it was influential (0 of 8 and 0 of 14 influential cases), while Gemini 3.1 Pro was accurate (0.96, [0.92, 1.0]); the same model made attribution statements for only 8% of the suggestions that were influential. neutral system note is influential for every model, and six of eight attribute the answer to it whether or not it was influential (2996% when non-influential). sections.title: G Training Details
sections.content: Training data. Table 14 lists the relabeled training examples for each model. Each model is labeled using its own counterfactual answers, so the number of influential examples varies across models. User suggestions on TriviaQA and MMLU are balanced jointly as one type. Within each type, we keep all influential examples and sample up to two non-influential examples per influential example; if type has fewer non-influential examples, we keep them all. No example exceeds the 8,192-token training length. Optimization. We train LoRA adapters of rank 64 (α = 128, no dropout) on all attention and MLP 4, projections for one epoch using learning rate 10 cosine schedule with 5% warmup, an effective batch size of 16, and bf16 precision. The loss is computed only on the completion, not the prompt. The three Qwen3-8B runs use seeds 42, 1, and 2, which determine the LoRA initialization and data Type of external information Qwen3-8B Qwen3-14B DeepSeek-R1-7B User suggestion (TriviaQA) 2,984 / 3,327 2,127 / 2,409 780 / 4,201 User suggestion (MMLU) 531 / 2,907 3,215 / 2,787 3,263 / 2,841 Retrieved passage 2,152 / 3,462 1,808 / 3,616 Tool output 1,530 / 3,060 1,202 / 2,404 Another AIs answer 6,050 / 4,691 1,792 / 9,203 3,123 / 2,611 3,633 / 1,739 3,050 / 2,311 Total 27,498 23,108 38,203 Table 14: CREDIT training examples (influential / noninfluential) by type of external information. DeepSeekR1-7B is DeepSeek-R1-Distill-Qwen-7B. order; all other models use seed 42. Generation. At evaluation, all models generate with reasoning enabled, using temperature 0.6, topp 0.95, top-k 20, fixed seed, and up to 8,192 new tokens. The 24 truncated outputs per model come from reasoning loops in both trained and untrained models and are excluded. To build training data, we sample with temperature 0.6 and top-p 0.95 (no top-k limit) and up to 6,144 new tokens: two responses per prompt for user suggestions and retrieved passages, and one for tool outputs and an20 other AIs answers, so each prompt contributes up to two training examples. Labels cost four counterfactual answers per TRAINING question: with one piece, counterfactual answer is the bare question, so the same four serve all types of external information and sampled responses of that question. This cost is paid once, in training; checking dependence at deployment would cost four extra generations for every answer. Model selection. We chose DeepSeek-R1-DistillQwen-7B, reasoning model distilled from DeepSeek-R1 (Guo et al., 2025) onto Qwen2.5 base (Yang et al., 2024), as the most improvable model in screen of untrained open models (balanced accuracy 0.55, compared with 0.71 for Qwen3-1.7B (Yang et al., 2025); the screen was separate, earlier run, so its value differs from the 0.60 in Table 1). The screen compared untrained models only and took place after CREDIT was frozen, but it used the TEST set; DeepSeeks TEST-set results are therefore not fully independent of its selection, and its FRESH-set and LARGE-set results are the cleaner estimates. Faithfulness-RL variant. We also tried an RL variant with the reward of Cheah et al. (2026), 1[attributed = influential] per rollout. It omits three parts of their setup: we do not balance influential and non-influential examples (so rarely attributing earns extra reward), we compute the loss on all completion tokens rather than on the explanation with the decision fixed, and we label influence on each rollout rather than once with the initial model. On the TEST set it stays near the untrained model (balanced accuracy 0.51; attribution in 2% of influential and 0% of non-influential cases), so we report it only here. rollout is influential if it gives the suggested answer and one counterfactual answer without the suggestion does not; attribution is read from the RELIED ON line by keyword rule (precision 1.00 and recall 0.670.89 against the LLM judge). The reward has no correctness term, and all completion tokens are credited. We train GRPO (Shao et al., 2024) with LoRA (rank 64, α = 128) from the untrained Qwen38B on 11,650 suggestion prompts (TriviaQA and MMLU, keeping prompts with usable counterfactual answers) with the attribution instruction: 8 rollouts per prompt at temperature 0.8, up to 4,096 6 (constant after new tokens, learning rate 2 10 5% warmup), KL coefficient 0.02, and the DAPO loss (Yu et al., 2025) with group-normalized rewards. We save checkpoint every 50 steps and select on the VALIDATION set with early stopping; the run stopped at step 283 of 400 when it reached its time limit. Validation balanced accuracy remains between 0.51 and 0.54 at every checkpoint (steps 50250), and we report step 50. Throughout training, attribution in influential rollouts stays at 2 5%, close to the untrained model; since about 79% of rollouts are non-influential, policy that never attributes already earns most of the reward, so the reward rarely observes the target behavior. Rollout accuracy also rises during training (cumulatively 0.63 after the first 20 steps and 0.79 by step 280): the policy can satisfy the reward without adopting the suggestion, making rollout non-influential and none correct.

sections.title: I Measurement Checks
sections.content: Influence labels. For each VALIDATION question, we sample eight answers with the suggestion and eight without it. Questions with influential responses show adoption-rate increases of +0.82 (untrained) and +0.86 (trained). For 9193% of these responses, the increase is at least 0.5. Responses labeled non-influential average +0.070.09. Populations. On the VALIDATION set, influence prevalence is similar across models (2933%). The ranking and gaps do not change when restricted to the 164 validation items that every model labels, or to the 136 on which all models agree. Answer matching. Influence labels require deciding whether an answer adopts the suggested answer. String matching fails on verbose answers: Vivaldi wrote it, not Bach contains the suggested answer, and counterfactual answer phrased as sentence may not contain any gold alias. An LLM judge therefore decides whether each final answer commits to the suggested answer (as opposed to mentioning it, hedging, or declining); training labels are built the same way. On Qwen3 test outputs the judge agrees with exact string matching on 9499% of labels, and on the LARGE set, whose answers are longer, on 8899%. Relabeling the training data changes 34% of influence labels. All reported models are trained and evaluated with these labels. Judge. Rescoring with keyword rule instead of the LLM judge gives identical test balanced accuracy for every Qwen3-8B model. The keyword rule ignores the fixed phrase in CREDITs target (I would not have given this answer without it), so the judges scores for trained models are not keyed to that phrase. Frontier-model attribution statements are free-form. The rule is too narrow, so their scores rely on the judge. For all types of external information, we also rescore every Qwen3 model without the judge, counting any attribution statement that mentions the external information or the suggested answer as selfattribution. This lenient rule favors terse lines that merely echo the external information. With LLM-matched labels, it changes one result: the 8B metadata gain shrinks from +0.24 to +0.13 ([0.07, 0.19]), because the untrained model copies the tag. All other gains keep their sign, and the 14B gains grow, most for user suggestions (+0.10 to +0.17, [0.07, 0.25]) and claimed expertise (+0.13 to +0.24, [0.18, 0.31]). Pipeline robustness. Unscored pieces (two of four counterfactual answers give as) are rare: 16% of user-suggestion pieces per model and question set, and at most 6.1% for DeepSeek on the LARGE set. We audited every point where the pipeline shortens text or falls back to default. The answer judge saw each question truncated to 80 characters (the datasets item identifier) for about quarter of questions; re-judging with full questions changes 1.11.5% of judgments and balanced accuracy by at most 0.003. response without parsable attribution statement counts as no attribution, and one without final-answer line as not giving as; excluding such responses instead changes balanced accuracy by at most 0.002 in every reported condition except one (DeepSeek-R1-7B with CREDIT on claimed expertise, 0.73 0.74). No attribution statement reaches the 1,000-character limit given to the judge, and judge outputs that cannot be parsed (at most 3 per run) are excluded rather than defaulted. Label reliability. To estimate label noise from the counterfactual answers, we resample them: for each scored piece with of counterfactual answers giving as, we draw rate from Beta(c + 2 , + 1 1 2 ), draw four new counterfactual answers, and relabel, keeping the sampled answer fixed. Of the labels, 9798% are unchanged (about 95% among agreeing answers), and predictor that reproduces the original labels exactly scores 0.95 0.97 balanced accuracy against resampled labels (0.890.95 among agreeing answers), well above CREDITs 0.790.90. Threshold sensitivity. Under strict rule (L = 0, = 4: influential only if no counterfactual answer gives as, non-influential only if all valid counterfactual answers give it or the answer does not adopt it), which keeps 8794% of CREDITs scored pieces, CREDITs balanced accuracy rises by 0.020.04 (to 0.810.94 across models and question sets), the untrained models change by at most 0.04, and every gain over the untrained model is preserved (changes of 0 to +0.04). The results do not hinge on the thresholds. Human validation of both judges. Annotators who did not see the judges decisions labeled stratified random sample for each judge, following written guidelines with worked examples. For self-attribution, two annotators labeled 87 statements from untrained and CREDIT Qwen models and frontier models, across the six types of external information evaluated on TEST questions and both judge verdicts. They agreed with the judge on 97.7% and 94.3% of statements (Cohens κ = 0.95 and 0.89) and with each other on 92.0% (κ = 0.84); on the 80 statements where both annotators agree, the judge agrees with them on all 80. Three of the second annotators five disagreements are statements that attribute the answer to the right information but name the wrong source (e.g., an answer key in the system prompt credited to the user), which the judge accepts; Section 7, where the source matters, additionally requires the right source. For answer matching, the same two annotators labeled 100 final answers (own answers and counterfactual answers; TriviaQA and TruthfulQA; both verdicts). They agreed with the judge on 89.0% and 99.0% of answers (κ = 0.78 and 0.98) and with each other on 88.0% (κ = 0.76); on the 88 answers where both annotators agree, the judge agrees with them on all 88. The remaining disagreements concentrate on long free-form TruthfulQA answers that hedge or list several options. How much is predictable from the question and external information? On answers that adopt the suggestion, classifier using only the question and the suggested answer predicts influence with AUROC 0.78. Adding the models own attribution statement raises it to 0.87 (VALIDATION set; question-bootstrap 95% CI of the gain [0.04, 0.18]). With access to whether the suggestion is correct, which deployed system lacks, the classifier reaches 0.91, and the attribution statement adds +0.03 ([0.004, 0.07]). We claim accurate selfattribution, not introspection.

sections.title: J Paraphrased Templates
sections.content: To check that the transfer results do not hinge on one wording, we rebuild every type of external information with second template (template B): tool call with JSON response, reference solution for evaluators (do not mention) system23 prompt note, bracketed gold_label metadata field, different chatbots earlier reply, and user claiming PhD on the topic. Table 16 reports Qwen3-8B on the TEST set. The trained types of external information improve as with template (tool output +0.21; another AIs answer +0.15). The gains on unseen types are smaller (metadata +0.04, claimed expertise +0.08), partly because the untrained model already scores higher on these wordings. Systemprompt notes again show little gain (+0.03).

sections.title: K Additional Results
sections.content: This appendix gives the full versions of results summarized in Sections 68. K.1 What Drives the Gain VFT with the attribution statement excluded from the loss. VFTs targets keep the models own final attribution statement, which for influential examples usually reads RELIED ON: none (59% of influential training examples). To rule out that this line trains the final answer toward chance, we retrain VFT on the same data with the attribution statement excluded from the loss. On the TEST set, the reasoning still acknowledges influential suggestions in 77% of cases and non-influential ones in 32% (balanced accuracy 0.73, vs. 0.74 for VFT), while the final line attributes none of the 52 influential and none of the 139 non-influential suggestions (0.50); on the FRESH set it attributes 4% of 201 influential suggestions (0.52). Acknowledgment in the reasoning does not reach the answer even when the answer is not trained toward none. In our experiments, supervising the user-facing statement works better than supervising the reasoning. With labels from the same counterfactual procedure, training the attribution statement into the final answer outperforms training it into the reasoning by +0.12 on the TEST set. VFTs reasoning acknowledges influential suggestions, but its final answer remains at chance. This holds whether the acknowledgment appears at the start of the reasoning or where the suggestion is first used. Supervising only the answer section suffices. Restricting the loss to tokens after the reasoning gives 0.88 balanced accuracy on the TEST set. The gain therefore does not come from training the reasoning. Restricting the loss further to the attribution statement alone is degenerate: the model stops writing its final answer (109 of 120 validation responses). One counterfactual answer already gives most of the gain. Labels from one counterfactual answer instead of four give similar test score (0.83; difference +0.03, [0.03, 0.09]). The ingredient that matters is supervising the final attribution statement with the models own counterfactual labels; more counterfactual answers make the labels more robust but are not essential. Untrained 14B fails by over-attributing suggestions. Untrained 14B often mentions the suggestion even when it was non-influential, in 21% of non-influential cases. Training makes it more selective, reducing this rate to 14%. For answers that agree with the suggestion, the harder stratum is correct suggestions: the model may already know the answer, so agreement alone says little about influence. In this stratum, CREDIT reaches 0.81, 0.78, and 0.71 at 8B (TEST, FRESH, LARGE), 0.80, 0.79, and 0.73 at 14B, and 0.74, 0.74, and 0.68 for DeepSeek, compared with 0.49 0.67 untrained. To test another model family, we apply the same pipeline, unchanged, to DeepSeek-R1-DistillLlama-8B (Guo et al., 2025) (one training seed). CREDIT raises balanced accuracy from 0.62 to 0.85 on the TEST set (omitted: 56% 19%; falsely attributed: 19% 12%), from 0.62 to 0.79 on the FRESH set, and from 0.59 to 0.79 on the LARGE set. Transfer follows the pattern of the Qwen models (TEST set, untrained CREDIT): tool outputs 0.60 0.80, another AIs answer 0.66 0.82, the unseen types question metadata 0.57 0.63 and claimed expertise 0.62 0.71, and no gain for system-prompt notes (0.51 0.50). Among answers that agree with the suggestion, where answer matching is at chance, CREDIT scores 0.77, 0.67, and 0.71 on the TEST, FRESH, and LARGE sets. Overall, CREDIT and the answer-matching rule are close on the TEST set (0.85 vs. 0.80; difference [0.01, 0.11]) and the FRESH set (0.79 vs. 0.78), and the matching rule is ahead on the LARGE set (0.82 vs. 0.79), as it is for DeepSeek-R1-7B (0.87 vs. 0.80). K.6 Transfer and System-Prompt Notes Instruction scope. The attribution instruction names information given by the user, or in documents or passages, which could exclude system prompts. With in the system prompt added to that list, system-prompt balanced accuracy rises only slightly: untrained Qwen3-8B 0.62 0.68 on the TEST set (+0.06, [0.03, 0.15]) and 0.59 0.63 on the FRESH set (+0.04, [0.00, 0.08]); CREDIT 0.63 0.66 (+0.02, [0.06, 0.10]) and 0.63 0.67 (+0.05, [0.01, 0.08]). K.7 Benchmark Passages On FaithEval, the 95% CIs of the three seeds gains over the untrained model are [0.03, 0.18], [0.03, 0.18], and [0.10, 0.24]. CREDIT reduces false attributions on FaithEval. The untrained model almost always attributes its answer to the passage, whether or not the passage was influential: 98% when influential and 65% when non-influential. The trained models continue to attribute their answers to the passage when it was influential (8692%) and mostly stop otherwise (2138%). For Qwen, CREDITs gain under competition comes mostly from fewer false attributions to the non-influential piece (8B: 15% 5%; 14B: 23% 7%); for DeepSeek, from naming the influential piece more often (28% 60%). Three competing pieces. With three competing pieces, the 8B gain holds (0.74 0.86 on the FRESH set; 0.78 0.85 on the TEST set), mainly through fewer false attributions (12% 4%); at 14B it is clear on the TEST set (0.77 0.84) but small on the FRESH set (0.78 0.79). Competing external information is scored piece by piece. With single piece of external information, the influential piece is always one whose answer the model gives, so matching the answer to the piece already identifies every influential case. We therefore also place two pieces with conflicting answers in one prompt. Matching remains informative there, since it points to the piece whose answer the model gives, but that piece may still be noninfluential, and the rule must know which source 27 proposed which answer. One piece gives the wrong answer and the other the correct one, delivered as user suggestion and tool output, or as another AIs answer and question metadata, in both role assignments. Each piece is scored separately. It is influential if the model gives its answer with both pieces present but rarely when only the other piece remains (four counterfactual answers). Because two pieces are present, an attribution counts only if names that pieces source, so naming the other piece is an error. Except for the multi-source variant  (Table 4)  , no model was trained on prompts with more than one piece. external information: with two pieces, identifying the influential one already requires separate set of counterfactual answers per piece (eight extra generations per answer in our setup), and pieces that matter only jointly would require counterfactual answers for combinations. CREDIT moves this cost to training: it uses counterfactual answering to build labels once and teaches the model to state, in single pass, what the intervention would have shown, and this single-pass self-attribution partially transfers to prompts with competing pieces (Section 7).

K.9 Why Not Re-Run the Model? Influence is defined by intervention, so re-running the model without each item of external information is the reference standard: single extra suggestion-free sample recovers our four-sample labels with balanced accuracy of about 0.97 (an optimistic estimate, since that sample is one of the four). It is, however, an external audit rather than an account given by the model. It needs one or more additional reasoning generations per candidate item of external information for every answer, it assumes each item of external information can be removed without changing the task (easy for users suggestion, not for system prompt, tool output inside an agent loop, or the conversation history), and it is unavailable to user who receives single response. Frontier models are accessed through their providers APIs under the providers terms of service. We release our code under Apache 2.0 and our derived data (prompts, model outputs, influence labels, and anonymized annotations) for research use under the terms of the source datasets. Data documentation. All data are in English. The questions are trivia and commonmisconception questions (TriviaQA, TruthfulQA), exam and science questions (MMLU, ARC), and commonsense questions (CommonsenseQA). External information is generated from templates  (Table 6)  or taken from FaithEval and RAMDocs. Question sets and their sizes are given in Table 5. 28 The questions concern public knowledge and contain no personal data beyond the names of public figures; we collected no data from people other than the annotations described below, and annotator identities are replaced by pseudonyms in the released files. Models and compute. The trained models have 8.2B (Qwen3-8B), 14.8B (Qwen3-14B), 7.6B (DeepSeek-R1-Distill-Qwen-7B), and 8.0B (DeepSeek-R1-Distill-Llama-8B) parameters; LoRA adds rank-64 adapters. Experiments ran on single NVIDIA GPUs with 48141 GB of memory. Across all experiments in this paper, including discarded runs, the jobs used about 650 GPU-hours. Generation uses vLLM 0.30.0, training uses Hugging Face Transformers 5.17.0, TRL 1.14.0, and PEFT 0.21.0 with PyTorch 2.13.0. Hyperparameters and model selection are described in Appendix G; all hyperparameters were fixed on the VALIDATION set, and results are single runs unless seeds are reported, with 95% bootstrap intervals that resample questions. Human annotation. Two of the authors labeled 87 attribution statements and 100 final answers for the human validation of both judges, and categorized 100 errors for the failure analysis, following written guidelines with worked examples that we release with the code (Appendices and I). The items are trivia and misconception questions with model responses; they contain no offensive content or personal data, and the annotation posed no risk to the annotators. No data were collected from people other than the authors. Use of AI assistants. We used AI assistants for coding, experiments, analysis, and writing.
